issues.legal_issue: Liability for mesne profits under a decree limited to defendants in possession depends on actual possession and enjoyment, rather than merely juridical ownership or an asserted derivative relationship.
material_facts: The decree directed an inquiry into mesne profits and made liable those defendants who had been in possession of the property.
The decree-holder’s opponent was found to have had sole actual control, management, and possession during the relevant period; the other defendant was not in actual possession.
The opponent had earlier denied being in possession and had not pleaded that his possession was derivative from the other defendant.
issues.conclusion: The defendant found in sole actual possession was liable for mesne profits for the period of that possession, except while the property was managed by the court-appointed receiver; the other defendant was not liable merely by reason of ownership or alleged juridical possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 2(12) of the Code of Civil Procedure, wrongful possession is the foundation of liability for mesne profits, which ordinarily follows actual possession and enjoyment. Where several persons jointly or concertedly keep a plaintiff out of possession, each participant may be liable even without actual possession; a court may impose joint and several liability or apportion liability where the material permits. The decree here limited liability to defendants found to have been in possession, which the Court construed as actual possession and enjoyment.

predicates.mesne_profits_execution_inquiry: A court is determining liability for mesne profits in an execution or related inquiry under a decree.
predicates.decree_limits_liability_to_possessors: The decree makes liable only defendants who were in possession of the property.
predicates.actual_possession_and_enjoyment: A defendant actually controlled, managed, possessed, and enjoyed the property during the relevant period.

issues.definition: When a mesne-profits inquiry under a decree limited to possessors concerns a defendant who actually possessed and enjoyed the property, that defendant is liable for mesne profits.

issues.legal_issue: A decree-holder is not required to set off a purchase-price deposit against one defendant’s mesne-profits liability merely because another defendant may also be liable or withdrew the deposit.
material_facts: The decree directed deductions from the purchase-price deposit for sums found due from specified defendants and directed payment of any balance to an assignee.
The decree did not direct that the deposit be set off against the mesne-profits liability of the defendant found in possession.
There was no evidence that the decree-holder and the assignee colluded in the withdrawal of the deposit.
The defendant asserting the proposed joint-liability theory had not pleaded it in the courts below.
issues.conclusion: The decree-holder was not required to allow the proposed set-off against the mesne-profits liability of the defendant in possession.
issues.legal_principle: Where several trespassers are jointly and severally liable for mesne profits, the plaintiff may elect to recover the whole from either, and the defendants’ inter se adjustment is ordinarily for them to resolve. A decree-holder need not accept a set-off in favour of one defendant absent a direction in the decree or evidence supporting the asserted collusion.

predicates.mesne_profits_execution_inquiry: A court is determining liability for mesne profits and adjustment of a deposit made toward the purchase price.
predicates.no_decree_directing_setoff: The decree does not direct that the purchase-price deposit be set off against the mesne-profits liability of the defendant from whom recovery is sought.
predicates.no_evidence_of_collusive_withdrawal: There is no evidence that the decree-holder colluded with another defendant in that defendant’s withdrawal of the deposit.

issues.definition: In a mesne-profits inquiry, if the decree does not direct the proposed set-off and collusive withdrawal is not shown, the decree-holder need not allow that set-off.

issues.legal_issue: Possession obtained during pending litigation under a sham arrangement by a person aware of the litigation is wrongful against the claimant from the start of that possession.
material_facts: The suit seeking specific performance and possession was already pending when the defendant obtained possession under an assignment of a lease found to be sham.
The defendant later acquired the property for another person using his own funds while the suit remained pending.
The defendant was aware that the property was the subject of litigation.
issues.conclusion: The defendant’s possession was wrongful against the plaintiff from its inception, rather than becoming wrongful only when the purchase price was deposited or the conveyance was executed.
issues.legal_principle: Wrongful possession is the foundation for mesne profits under Section 2(12) of the Code of Civil Procedure. On these facts, possession obtained during pending litigation through a sham lease, by a person conscious that he was purchasing a litigation, was wrongful against the plaintiff from the outset.

rule.if: mesne_profits_claim and possession_obtained_during_pending_suit and sham_possession_arrangement and possessor_aware_of_litigation

predicates.mesne_profits_claim: A claimant seeks mesne profits for another person’s possession of property.
predicates.possession_obtained_during_pending_suit: The possessor entered the property while a suit concerning the claimant’s rights to it was pending.
predicates.sham_possession_arrangement: The possessor relied on an arrangement that was found to be sham.
predicates.possessor_aware_of_litigation: The possessor knew that the property was the subject of litigation when entering possession.

issues.definition: If possession relevant to a mesne-profits claim began during pending litigation under a sham arrangement and the possessor knew of the litigation, the possession is wrongful from its beginning.

issues.legal_issue: For the three-year limit on future mesne profits, the relevant decree is the final appellate decree granting possession and directing the inquiry, and the period ends at the first applicable cutoff.
material_facts: The trial court decreed specific performance and mesne profits, but the appellate court initially dismissed the suit.
The Supreme Court later allowed the plaintiff’s appeal, granted specific performance and possession upon deposit, and directed an inquiry into mesne profits.
Possession was delivered pursuant to that final decree before three years had elapsed from its date.
The mesne-profits award covered the period from the defendant’s entry into possession until delivery, excluding the period of the receiver’s management.
issues.conclusion: The three-year period under Order XX Rule 12(1)(c) ran from the final appellate decree; the lower courts acted consistently with the decree and the rule in awarding profits until delivery of possession, which occurred within that period.
issues.legal_principle: Order XX Rule 12(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure allows an inquiry into mesne profits from the institution of the suit until delivery of possession, relinquishment with notice through the court, or three years from the date of the decree, whichever occurs first. The decree referred to is the final decree for possession and mesne profits, including an appellate decree. In Chitturi Subbanna v. Kudapa Subbanna, the Court stated that a decree directing an inquiry must be construed consistently with Rule 12(1)(c), so that the decree-holder cannot obtain profits beyond the applicable limit.

predicates.suit_for_possession_and_mesne_profits: The proceeding seeks possession of immovable property and mesne profits.
predicates.final_appellate_decree_grants_possession: A final appellate decree grants possession and directs an inquiry into mesne profits.
predicates.possession_delivered_before_three_year_c: Possession is delivered before three years have elapsed from the final appellate decree.

issues.definition: In a possession-and-mesne-profits proceeding, when a final appellate decree grants possession and delivery occurs before the three-year cutoff, mesne profits end at the first applicable cutoff.

issues.legal_issue: Where the accounts and other evidence of actual profits are unreliable, the rental fixed for the property by a court-appointed receiver may be used as the basis for assessing mesne profits.
material_facts: The accounts and profit-and-loss statements prepared for tax purposes were found unreliable and did not prove the profits derived from operating the factory.
The plaintiff did not produce cogent evidence of the profits earned while operating the factory.
The receiver had leased the factory to the defendant at a stated annual rent, and there was no reliable competing evidence of its rental value or profits.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in assessing mesne profits by reference to the annual rent fixed under the receiver’s lease.
issues.legal_principle: Mesne profits are in the nature of damages, and no invariable rule governs their assessment; the court may assess them according to the justice of the case. Where the evidence of actual profits is unreliable and the receiver’s rental is the only reliable evidence, that rental may reasonably represent the property’s value for assessing mesne profits.

predicates.mesne_profits_assessment: A court is assessing the amount of mesne profits payable for property.
predicates.actual_profit_evidence_unreliable: The evidence offered to establish actual profits is found unreliable or insufficient.
predicates.receiver_rental_is_reliable_evidence: A rental fixed under a lease by a court-appointed receiver is reliable and is the only reliable evidence of the property’s rental value.

issues.definition: When actual-profit evidence is unreliable and the receiver’s rental is reliable evidence in a mesne-profits assessment, the court may assess profits by reference to that rental.

issues.legal_issue: Interest is properly included in mesne profits where a claimant was kept out of possession after prolonged litigation, notwithstanding the claimant’s use of money intended for the purchase price.
material_facts: The plaintiff obtained possession only after protracted litigation.
The trial court awarded interest on assessed mesne profits, while the High Court reduced the rate partly because the plaintiff had use of the money deposited toward the purchase price.
The Supreme Court restored the trial court’s interest award and directed continuing interest on the outstanding amount until payment.
issues.conclusion: Interest at the trial court’s rate was payable as part of the mesne profits, including on the outstanding amount until payment.
issues.legal_principle: Mesne profits are in the nature of damages, and their assessment may be moulded to the justice of the case. The Court held that prolonged litigation before the plaintiff obtained possession supported the trial court’s award of interest; the plaintiff’s use of the purchase-price funds did not justify the reduction made by the High Court.

predicates.mesne_profits_assessed: A court has assessed mesne profits payable for property.
predicates.claimant_kept_out_of_possession_after_pr: The claimant obtained possession only after being kept out of possession through prolonged litigation.

issues.definition: When mesne profits are assessed for a claimant kept out of possession after prolonged litigation, the award carries interest.

issues.legal_issue: Interest may be awarded as restitution on money withdrawn under a decree that is later reversed or varied, when the interest is consequential on that reversal or variation.
material_facts: The receiver collected rent from the defendant and deposited it in court.
After the plaintiff’s suit was dismissed on appeal, the defendant withdrew the deposited rent.
The plaintiff later succeeded in the Supreme Court, and the defendant redeposited the money only after that decree.
The trial court allowed interest for the period between withdrawal and redeposit, but the High Court disallowed it on the stated ground that the Supreme Court did not award it.
issues.conclusion: The defendant was liable for interest on the withdrawn sum for the period between withdrawal and redeposit by way of restitution.
issues.legal_principle: Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure authorizes orders for restitution consequential on variation or reversal of a decree, including orders for interest, damages, compensation, and mesne profits. In the absence of an express or implied prohibition in the Supreme Court decree, interest could be allowed on the withdrawn deposit as restitution.

predicates.restitution_claim_after_decree_reversal_: A party seeks restitution after a decree has been reversed or varied.
predicates.money_withdrawn_under_earlier_decree: A party withdrew money deposited in court following the earlier decree and later redeposited it after reversal or variation.
predicates.interest_is_consequential: Interest is sought for the period during which the withdrawn money was withheld and is consequential on the reversal or variation.

issues.definition: If restitution is sought after reversal or variation and a party withheld money withdrawn under the earlier decree, restitution may include consequential interest.

issues.legal_issue: A defendant liable for mesne profits may receive a deduction reflecting interest on purchase-price money that the decree-holder withdrew and later redeposited.
material_facts: The plaintiff withdrew part of the purchase-price deposit after his suit was dismissed on appeal.
He redeposited that sum after succeeding in the Supreme Court.
The defendant was liable for mesne profits during a period that overlapped the withdrawal.
The Court considered it fair to deduct interest on the withdrawn sum for the relevant period, excluding the period during which the property was managed by the receiver.
issues.conclusion: The defendant was allowed a deduction from mesne profits for interest on the purchase-price sum withdrawn and later redeposited.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing the parties’ monetary obligations, the Court allowed a fair deduction for the period during which the decree-holder had withdrawn and retained the purchase-price money, subject to excluding the receiver-management period.

rule.if: mesne_profits_execution_inquiry and decree_holder_withdrew_purchase_deposit and deposit_later_redeposited and defendant_liable_for_mesne_profits

predicates.mesne_profits_execution_inquiry: A court is determining monetary obligations in an execution or related inquiry under a decree.
predicates.decree_holder_withdrew_purchase_deposit: The decree-holder withdrew money deposited toward the purchase price after an adverse judgment.
predicates.deposit_later_redeposited: The decree-holder later redeposited that money after succeeding on appeal.
predicates.defendant_liable_for_mesne_profits: The defendant is liable for mesne profits during a period that includes the time the deposit was withdrawn.

issues.definition: In a mesne-profits inquiry, if the decree-holder withdrew and later redeposited the purchase-price money and the defendant is liable for mesne profits, the award is reduced by interest on the withdrawn deposit.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court should not interfere with a lower court’s discretionary decision on costs absent a sufficient reason to do so.
material_facts: The lower courts denied the plaintiff costs relating to the inquiry into mesne profits and the ensuing appeal.
The defendant had died, and the respondent in the appeal was his widow.
The Supreme Court found no reason to disturb the lower courts’ exercise of discretion on costs.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the lower courts’ decision to deny those costs.
issues.legal_principle: The award of costs was a matter within the lower courts’ discretion, and the Supreme Court found no basis to interfere in the circumstances.

predicates.appeal_challenges_discretionary_cost_ord: An appeal challenges a lower court’s discretionary decision on costs.
predicates.lower_court_exercised_cost_discretion: The lower court considered the costs issue and exercised its discretion in deciding whether to award costs.
predicates.no_sufficient_reason_to_interfere: The circumstances do not provide a sufficient reason for the reviewing court to disturb that exercise of discretion.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a discretionary costs order, the lower court exercised its discretion, and no sufficient reason to interfere exists, the order is left undisturbed.
